questions.prompt: A background agent's Write or Edit is refused when any of three tests matches: the target is the same file on disk as a protected settings file (device and inode, after links), the Unicode-folded name of its path or of its real path is a protected name, or a settings file name is reached through `..`. Keep all three tests, or drop the same-file test?

options.label: Keep all three tests, as the plan specifies
options.pros: The same-file test is the only one of the three that sees a hard link to a settings file and any alias of an existing settings file that the name fold does not reproduce, because it asks the file system rather than reading the spelling (plan lines 189 to 192). The folded-name test then covers files that do not exist yet, which no same-file test can see, so between them the editing tools become a real refusal rather than a second name guard, and the hard-link gap that src/lib/real-path-confinement.js states open is closed for these files.
options.cons: It adds a device-and-inode helper to the one hook Claude Code loads, with two failure rules of its own that each had to be designed so they never refuse every agent write (a file system that reports inode 0, and a protected file whose status call fails), plus a file-status call on every background agent's editing target and one more per protected file, up to seven, whenever the target already exists, timed against the plan's 50 millisecond stop. The routes only this test closes are deliberate evasions, which your ruling already assigns to isolating agents rather than to this hook.
options.description: Read at plans/implementation/a-background-agent-cannot-change-claude-codes-settings.md line 188, the editing tools' three tests, and line 1102, Decision 18, which keeps both the name test and the same-file test.

options.label: Drop the same-file test and match folded names only
options.pros: Less code and fewer failure modes in the one hook Claude Code loads: no device-and-inode helper, no inode-0 rule, no rule for a protected file whose status call fails, and no extra file-status calls per protected file on each agent write. The folded name of the path and of its real path still refuses every direct write, every letter case, the long s, Windows trailing dots and stream suffixes, and every file or folder link, which covers the honest mistakes the plan's tests enumerate; a hard link into a settings file has to be made deliberately, and your ruling puts deliberate evasion on agent isolation.
options.cons: A hard link to a settings file, made from anywhere in the project, becomes an open route on the editing tools as well as on the shell, and so does any alias of an existing settings file that the Unicode fold plus lower case does not reproduce. The plan's claim that the editing tools refuse by file identity (lines 42 to 46 and 141 to 144) would have to be narrowed to a name guard, and the hard-link gap stated in src/lib/real-path-confinement.js would stay open for these files too.
options.description: This option is the plan's three tests without the first one, described at line 189.

questions.prompt: Your order named Claude Code's settings files; this plan also refuses a background agent's write of CTOC's own .ctoc/settings.json, which holds the auto-push switch, the deployment dry-run switch and the command run at verification, so the deployment-setup agent stops saving its configuration and reports it for the main session to write with your OK. Protect .ctoc/settings.json as well?

options.label: Protect .ctoc/settings.json too, as the plan specifies
options.pros: The file holds three switches that later calls obey without asking anyone: git.autoPushEnabled, the ship switch src/lib/settings.js reads; the deployment block, whose dry_run false makes src/lib/deployment.js really push; and general.entry_point, the command src/lib/app-runner.js runs at the verification step. A background agent that changes any of them, by mistake or otherwise, either sends unreviewed work out or runs a command of its choosing at the next verification, and a push or a deploy cannot be taken back by a later plan. Of the agent definitions only deployment-setup is told to write this file, so the relay changes one agent's workflow.
options.cons: The deployment-setup agent can no longer save its own configuration: it reports the deployment block, and the main session shows it to you and writes it only with your OK, one more question each time a deployment is configured. A future plan whose build must change .ctoc/settings.json is refused to the background builder and has to be finished in the main session. And the guard is partial: the sandbox leaves .ctoc writable to the shell, so there only the text rule stands, which misses a script, a path in a variable or a git checkout that rewrites the file.
options.description: Read at plans/implementation/a-background-agent-cannot-change-claude-codes-settings.md lines 113 to 120 (what the file holds), line 161 (row d of the protected files) and lines 626 to 649 (the deployment-setup agent's new paragraph); the three readers confirmed at src/lib/settings.js:305, src/lib/deployment.js:59 and src/lib/app-runner.js:120.

options.label: Protect only Claude Code's settings files, as your order named
options.pros: Keeps this change inside the gap you measured and ordered closed: the two .claude settings files and the user-level settings file, which decide the hooks, environment and permissions of every later call. The deployment-setup agent keeps saving its configuration in one step with no relay and no extra question to you, and a background builder can still change .ctoc/settings.json when a plan declares it. Against a deliberate agent your ruling already puts the real barrier on isolating agents, and the shell route into .ctoc stays open to anything the text rule cannot read under either option.
options.cons: Any background agent can rewrite .ctoc/settings.json with Write or Edit, by mistake or otherwise: turn on auto-push, set the deployment dry-run switch to false, or replace the command run at verification. The first sends unreviewed work out past your ship switch and the second makes the pipeline really deploy, neither of which a later plan can take back. The plan's title, row d of its protected files, the deployment-setup paragraph and its tests would all have to be cut back to match.
